title: Predicting expression-altering promoter mutations with deep learning
source_note: Not the full paper: no access to the full text, so these notes are based only on the publicly available abstract and metadata (PubMed). Details from the main text and figures are missing.

items.q: What gap does this paper address?
items.a: Exome sequencing currently diagnoses only a minority of patients with rare genetic diseases. This suggests that other, unrecognized pathogenic variants may sit in noncoding sequence.
items.info: This file has only the abstract and PubMed/Crossref metadata. The full text was not available.

items.a: PromoterAI is a deep neural network that identifies noncoding promoter variants that dysregulate gene expression.
items.info: The abstract does not give the model's architecture, training data or input features.
items.concl: PromoterAI accurately identifies promoter variants that alter gene expression.

items.q: How did they show that PromoterAI predictions match real expression changes?
items.a: Promoter variants predicted to alter expression produced outlier expression at both the RNA and protein levels in thousands of individuals.
items.info: The abstract does not name the cohorts or datasets used, or the exact number of individuals.

items.q: What does population genetics say about predicted expression-altering promoter variants?
items.a: These variants experience strong negative selection in human populations.
items.info: The abstract does not say how selection was measured.

items.q: Are these variants enriched in patients with rare diseases?
items.a: Yes. In patients with rare diseases, clinically relevant genes are enriched for promoter variants predicted to alter expression.
items.info: The abstract does not give the patient cohort or the effect sizes.

items.q: How did they test the functional impact of the variants experimentally?
items.a: They validated the functional impact of the variants with reporter assays.
items.info: The abstract does not give the assay type, cell lines or number of variants tested.

items.q: How much of the rare disease genetic burden comes from promoter variation?
items.a: The authors estimate that promoter variation accounts for 6% of the genetic burden associated with rare diseases.
items.info: This is an estimate. The abstract does not explain how it was calculated.
items.concl: Promoter variants are a meaningful but minor part of rare disease genetics, and exome sequencing misses them.

items.a: Humans. The study covers human populations and patients with rare diseases.
items.info: The MeSH terms are Humans, Deep Learning, Exome Sequencing, Gene Expression Regulation, Mutation, Promoter Regions, Genetic, and Rare Diseases.

items.text: Read the full text for the PromoterAI architecture, training data, how the promoter region was defined, the cohorts used for RNA and protein outliers, and how the 6% burden estimate was calculated. Could the approach be applied to non-human genomes such as zebrafish or Astyanax?
